Text 1
Philosopher John Rawls's most significant contribution centers on the concept of moral intuition. He argues that there are certain ethical judgments that all people, including moral philosophers, recognize instinctively as correct, regardless of their theoretical commitments: among them, that slavery is wrong, or that people deserve equal basic liberties. Rawls's systematic work on moral intuition may appear straightforward but was actually revolutionary.

Text 2
Moral relativism is a philosophical position maintaining that we cannot determine universal ethical truths because moral judgments are entirely dependent on cultural context. During a debate, John Rawls once argued against this position by pointing to widespread condemnation of genocide and saying, 'Some moral facts transcend cultural boundaries.' Many philosophers immediately dismiss this argument (Bernard Williams called it 'a philosophically naive oversimplification') but struggle to explain precisely why the argument is unconvincing.
